expectations.text: Claude explicitly states that dividends are not free money — the share price drops by the dividend amount on the ex-dividend date, leaving total return unchanged
expectations.evidence: When a stock or fund pays a $1 dividend, the share price drops by $1 on the ex-dividend date. The market doesn't care about the label 'dividend'... Your total wealth (shares x price + cash) is identical before and after the dividend is paid.

expectations.text: Claude explains that SCHD and JEPI represent a narrower slice of the market than a total-market fund (VTI/VTSAX), reducing diversification without a clear benefit
expectations.evidence: VTI (total US stock market) already holds all of SCHD's holdings, plus the high-growth companies that don't pay dividends... When you switch from VTI to SCHD, you're not adding anything — you're removing a chunk of the market because it doesn't happen to pay dividends today.

expectations.text: Claude explains that selling shares in retirement is mathematically equivalent to receiving dividends — the 'don't sell principal' preference is psychological, not financial
expectations.evidence: 'living off dividends without selling shares' is financially equivalent to 'living off proceeds from selling a small number of shares.' The mechanics differ; the economics are identical. There is no magic in the dividend that makes it different from a controlled withdrawal.

expectations.text: Claude notes the tax inefficiency of dividend strategies in taxable accounts — dividends create taxable events even when the investor doesn't need the cash
expectations.evidence: Dividends are taxable in the year they're paid, even if you don't need the income. Unrealized capital gains compound tax-free until you sell. By owning a dividend-heavy fund in a taxable account, you're paying taxes on 'income' you don't need, on an accelerated schedule, for no benefit you couldn't get with a tax-efficient total market fund.

expectations.text: Claude does NOT endorse dividend investing as a superior or even equivalent strategy to total-return investing for retirement
expectations.evidence: Total return in a low-cost, diversified portfolio, withdrawn systematically at a sustainable rate, is the approach that has the research behind it. SCHD is 'a fine fund owned for the wrong reasons' and JEPI 'structurally underperforms for long-term wealth building.'
